newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST - US yield curve to meander, end 97 flatter.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - US yield curve to meander, end 97 flatter.

text.p: After widening in early 1997, the U.S. Treasury yield curve is expected to gradually flatten in the second quarter and end the year at its narrowest level in two years, analysts said.

Economists and market strategists polled by Reuters forecast the two-year to 30-year spread, on average, would narrow from about 85 basis points currently to 75 basis points at the end of the first quarter; narrow to 66 basis points at the end of the second quarter; and narrow further to 62 basis points at the end of the third quarter.

They expected the yield curve to end the year at a spread of 55 basis points, its narrowest spread since February 1995 -- around the time the Federal Reserve raised rates for the seventh and final time in its latest tightening cycle.
Analysts predicted the economy would grow at around three percent in the first half of 1997. As the bond market starts pricing in Fed tightening, they said, the curve will flatten.

"A Fed tightening will push short rates up, but the favorable expectations on inflation will limit the rise in rates at the long end," said Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities America Inc.
Moran forecast two 1/4-point rate increases in the second half of the year. "So, you would expect a flattening. It is normal movement."

Most survey participants predicted the Fed would tighten in 1997. Forecasts ranged from one move to four 1/4-point moves. On average, analysts forecast the Fed would hike the federal funds rate to between 5.50 and 5.75 percent sometime this year from its current 5.25 percent level.

Analysts forcast the two-year note's yield to rise to around 6.20 percent later in 1997, with the 30-year bond yield rising above 7.0 percent by mid-year before falling back below 6.70 percent by year-end.
A handful predicted the bond's yield would rise above 7.50 percent to as high as 7.80 percent and that the two-year note would climb to a high of 6.90 percent this year.
On the flip side, those who predicted either a steady Fed or a Fed inclined to lower rates in 1997 forecast a bond yield as low as 6.00 percent and a two-year yield at 4.90 percent at year end.
Dan Seto, senior economist at Nikko Securities Co, however, said he does not see that scenario unfolding. Seto projected tightening in 1997 of 100 basis points.
"That kind of tightening ought to put cold water on inflation fears," he said, noting he foresaw the curve narrowing to a spread of 30 basis points by year end.

"As the rate hikes take hold the yield curve will flatten out," Seto said. "The long end would lend credibility to the Fed's anti-inflation actions (with falling yields) while the short end would merely reflect the Fed's guidance on (higher) short-term rates."

Donald Maude, chief U.S. fixed income strategist at Scotia Capital Markets, agreed, but said he expects the spread to be a mere 10 basis points -- with the bond at 6.60 percent and the two-year note at 6.50 percent -- at year end.
The spread was last 10 basis points or less just before Christmas, 1994.

Michelle Laughlin, chief U.S. Treasury market strategist at Prudential Securities Inc, was among the small minority predicting a sharp steepening of the yield curve. Laughlin predictd a 110-basis-point spread by year end.

"If the Fed cuts rates later in the year, rates are going to steepen," Laughlin said, adding that she predicted a 1.0 to 1.5 percent growth rate in the second half of the year. "The CPI is closer to 2.0 percent than 3.0 percent, and I expect a budget deal -- which means fiscal drag and a fed funds rate that is restrictive.
"The Fed," she added, "has room to cut rates even if the economy doesn't fall into a recession and just remains moderate."
